q: The isomerization A → B is first order. The boxes show the reaction mixture at t = 0 and at t = 20 s. How many A molecules will be left at t = 60 s?
h: For a first-order reaction the half-life does not depend on how much A is left. Read the half-life from the two boxes.
w: Half of the 16 A molecules reacted in 20 s, so t1/2 = 20 s. 60 s is three half-lives: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2, leaving 2 A and 14 B. Losing 8 A every 20 s (a constant rate) would be zero order and give 0 A; 4 A is only two half-lives.
x: This assumes A is used up at a constant rate, which is zero order. A first-order reaction slows as A runs low.
This counts only two half-lives. Divide 60 s by the half-life again.
This counts four half-lives. Check how long one half-life is from the boxes.

q: The reaction 2 AB(g) → A<sub>2</sub>(g) + B<sub>2</sub>(g) runs in a 1.0 L flask. Each molecule drawn represents 0.010 mol. What is the average rate of formation of A<sub>2</sub> over the first 5.0 s?
h: Count the A<sub>2</sub> molecules that appear, turn that into a change in molarity, then divide by the time.
w: Three A2 molecules form, so Δ[A2] = 3 × 0.010 mol / 1.0 L = 0.030 M. Rate = 0.030 M / 5.0 s = 6.0×10−3 M s−1. 1.2×10−2 M s−1 is the rate at which AB disappears (6 AB used); 3.0×10−2 is Δ[A2] without dividing by time.
x: Six AB molecules were used, but only three A₂ formed. This is the rate of loss of AB.
Three A₂ molecules formed. There is no need to divide by the coefficient 2 here.
0.030 M is the change in concentration. A rate also needs the time.

q: The overall reaction A<sub>2</sub> + 2 B → 2 AB occurs in two steps. The boxes show the mixture at the start, midway, and at the end. Based on the boxes, which species is a reaction intermediate?
h: An intermediate is made in one step and used up in a later step, so it is not part of the overall equation.
w: Single A atoms are absent at the start, appear midway, and are gone at the end, so they are made in one step and used up in the next: they are the intermediate. A2 and B are reactants that are only used up, and AB is the product that only builds up.
x: A₂ is present at the start and is only used up. That makes it a reactant.
AB keeps building up and is in the overall equation as the product.
B is present at the start and is only used up. That makes it a reactant.

q: The box shows the equilibrium mixture for 2 A(g) ⇌ A<sub>2</sub>(g) in a 1.0 L flask; each particle represents 0.10 mol. The volume is suddenly cut to 0.50 L at constant temperature. Which statement describes the mixture right after the change?
c: Q<sub>c</sub> = 0.42; the reaction shifts right, forming more A<sub>2</sub>.
Q<sub>c</sub> = 0.83; there is no shift, since no particles were added.
Q<sub>c</sub> = 1.7; the reaction shifts left, forming more A.
Q<sub>c</sub> = 0.42; the reaction shifts left, forming more A.
h: Find K<sub>c</sub> from the box first. Halving the volume doubles every concentration; recompute Q<sub>c</sub> = [A<sub>2</sub>]/[A]<sup>2</sup>.
w: At 1.0 L, [A] = 0.60 M and [A2] = 0.30 M, so Kc = 0.30/(0.60)2 = 0.83. At 0.50 L, [A] = 1.20 M and [A2] = 0.60 M, so Qc = 0.60/(1.20)2 = 0.42. Q < K, so the reaction shifts right toward A2, the side with fewer gas particles. The counts are the same, but the concentrations are not.
x: The particle counts did not change, but the concentrations doubled. Q depends on concentration.
Doubling the concentrations does not double Q here, because [A] is squared in the denominator.
Q is right, but compare it with K again. When Q is smaller than K, products must form.

q: The box shows an equilibrium mixture for A(g) + B(g) ⇌ AB(g) in a 1.0 L flask; each particle represents 0.10 mol. Three more B atoms are added at constant volume and temperature. Which set of counts represents the mixture after equilibrium is re-established?
h: Get K<sub>c</sub> from the box. Then check which set of counts conserves atoms and gives the same K<sub>c</sub>.
w: From the box, Kc = 0.40/(0.40 × 0.30) = 3.3. Adding B makes Q < K, so some A and B combine. With one more AB formed, the counts are 3 A, 5 B, 5 AB: Kc = 0.50/(0.30 × 0.50) = 3.3. The unchanged mixture (4 A, 6 B, 4 AB) has Q = 1.7, and having all three added B react overshoots (Q = 23).
x: This is the mixture before any shift. Q is now smaller than K, so it cannot stay this way.
Adding a reactant does not push the reaction toward the reactants.
Not all of the added B reacts. Check Q for these counts against K.

q: The box shows a solution of the weak acid HA at equilibrium (water molecules omitted). What is the percent ionization of HA?
h: Percent ionization compares the HA that ionized with ALL the HA that was put in, ionized or not.
w: Two HA ionized (2 A− and 2 H3O+), and 8 HA remain, so 10 HA were present at first. Percent ionization = 2/10 × 100% = 20%. 25% divides by only the 8 un-ionized HA, and 80% is the fraction that did not ionize.
x: This divides by the HA left over. Use the HA that was present before ionizing.
Each ionized HA makes one A⁻ and one H₃O⁺. Count the acid molecules, not all the ions.
This is the part of the acid that did not ionize.

q: H<sub>2</sub>A is a weak diprotic acid with K<sub>a1</sub> = 1×10<sup>−4</sup> and K<sub>a2</sub> = 1×10<sup>−9</sup>. Each box has the same amount of acid (water omitted, and the amount of ionization is exaggerated so it can be seen). Which box best represents an aqueous solution of H<sub>2</sub>A at equilibrium?
h: K<sub>a1</sub> is small, so most H<sub>2</sub>A stays intact. K<sub>a2</sub> is far smaller still: how much A<sup>2−</sup> should you expect?
w: Because Ka1 is small, most of the acid stays as H2A, with a little HA− and an equal amount of H3O+. Ka2 is 105 times smaller, so essentially no A2− forms: box I. Box III treats the first step as strong, box II gives the second step a large share, and box IV removes both protons at once while skipping HA−.
x: Box II has a lot of A²⁻. With Ka2 = 1×10⁻⁹ the second ionization is tiny.
Box III has no H₂A left, as if the first ionization were strong. Ka1 = 1×10⁻⁴ is a weak acid.
Protons come off one at a time, so A²⁻ can only form from HA⁻. Box IV has A²⁻ but no HA⁻.

q: Each box shows a buffer made from the weak acid HA (pK<sub>a</sub> = 4.74) and its conjugate base A<sup>−</sup>, in equal volumes (water and Na<sup>+</sup> omitted). Which buffer has a pH closest to 5.2?
h: Use pH = pK<sub>a</sub> + log([A<sup>−</sup>]/[HA]). A pH above the pK<sub>a</sub> needs more of which species?
w: pH = 4.74 + log(A−/HA). Box I: 4.74 + log(2/6) = 4.26. Box II: 4.74 + log(4/4) = 4.74. Box III: 4.74 + log(6/2) = 5.22. Box IV: 4.74 + log(7/1) = 5.59. Box I has the ratio upside down.
x: Box I has more HA than A⁻, so its pH is below the pKa.
Box II has equal HA and A⁻, so its pH equals the pKa.
Box IV has too high a ratio of A⁻ to HA. Its pH is near 5.6.

q: Solutions are mixed to give the M<sup>2+</sup> and X<sup>2−</sup> ions shown (spectator ions and water omitted). Each ion represents 1.0×10<sup>−5</sup> M, and K<sub>sp</sub> of MX = 3.0×10<sup>−10</sup>. After precipitation reaches equilibrium, which ions remain dissolved?
h: First compare Q with K<sub>sp</sub>. Each MX that precipitates removes one M<sup>2+</sup> and one X<sup>2−</sup>; stop when the ion product equals K<sub>sp</sub>.
w: Q = (6×10−5)(4×10−5) = 2.4×10−9 > Ksp, so MX precipitates. Removing 3 of each ion leaves (3×10−5)(1×10−5) = 3.0×10−10 = Ksp, so 3 M2+ and 1 X2− remain. A slightly soluble salt never removes every X2−, and stopping at 4 and 2 leaves Q = 8.0×10−10, still above Ksp.
x: A precipitate is in equilibrium with its ions, so some X²⁻ stays dissolved.
Q for these ions is larger than Ksp, so some MX must precipitate.
For these counts the ion product is still larger than Ksp, so more MX precipitates.

q: Pure solid silver chromate, Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>, is shaken with pure water until the solution is saturated. Which box best represents the dissolved ions (water and undissolved solid omitted)?
h: Write the dissolution equation. How many Ag<sup>+</sup> ions enter the solution for each CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ion?
w: Ag2CrO4(s) ⇌ 2 Ag+(aq) + CrO42−(aq), so dissolving the pure solid gives twice as many Ag+ as CrO42−: box I (4 Ag+, 2 CrO42−), which is also electrically neutral. Box II shows a 1 : 1 ratio, box III the ratio reversed, and box IV a 3 : 1 ratio.
x: A 1 to 1 ratio ignores the subscript 2 on Ag. Check the charges too.
This reverses the ratio. Look at which ion has the subscript 2 in the formula.
This has too many Ag⁺ ions for the CrO₄²⁻ present, so the charges do not balance.

q: The boxes show a gas-phase reaction in a rigid container at constant temperature. The reaction is exothermic because bonds form. Which statement is correct?
c: ΔS < 0; it is spontaneous only at low temperature.
ΔS > 0; it is spontaneous at all temperatures.
ΔS < 0; it is spontaneous only at high temperature.
ΔS > 0; it is spontaneous only at high temperature.
h: Compare the number of independent gas particles before and after. Then use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with ΔH < 0.
w: Eight gas atoms become four molecules, so there are fewer independent gas particles and ΔS < 0. With ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative only when T is small enough: ΔS < 0; spontaneous only at low temperature. At high T the −TΔS term (now positive) wins and ΔG becomes positive.
x: Fewer gas particles means fewer ways to arrange the system, so entropy goes down.
With ΔS negative, −TΔS is positive and grows as T rises, so high T works against this reaction.
Count the gas particles in each box. Going from eight separate atoms to four molecules lowers the entropy.

q: A strip of metal M is placed in a silver nitrate solution. The boxes show the cations in solution before and some time later (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ions and water omitted). How many Ag atoms plated out, and how many electrons were transferred in all?
h: Each Ag<sup>+</sup> that leaves the solution gains one electron. Each M atom that dissolves becomes M<sup>2+</sup>.
w: The Ag+ count drops from 8 to 2, so 6 Ag+ were reduced to Ag atoms, gaining one electron each: 6 Ag atoms; 6 electrons. These 6 electrons came from 3 M atoms, each losing 2 to become M2+, which keeps the solution's positive charge at 8+. Counting 2 electrons per Ag doubles the total, and the 2 Ag+ left are still in solution.
x: Each Ag⁺ needs only one electron to become Ag. The 2 electrons per atom belong to M.
Three M²⁺ ions formed, but count the Ag⁺ ions that disappeared.
The 2 Ag⁺ ions shown are still dissolved. Count how many were removed.
